# Today's Learning Goals

## By the end of this lecture, we will be able to...

- Calculate marginal distributions from a joint distribution of random variables.
- Describe the probabilistic consequences of working with independent random variables.

## And...

- Calculate and describe covariance in multivariate cases (i.e., with more than one random variable).
- Calculate and describe two mainstream correlation metrics: Pearson's correlation and Kendall's $\tau_K$.

# Outline

1. Joint Distributions
2. Independence and Dependence Concepts

## 1. Joint Distributions

<br>

- So far, we have only considered one random variable at a time which has an <span style="color: purple;">univariate distribution</span>.
- However, we very often have <span style="color: purple;">more than one random variable</span>.

![](images/panda.png){fig-align="center" width=22%}

### Coins come again!

- Consider <span style="color: purple;">two independent fair coins</span> (i.e., two independent Bernoulli random variables!).
- The sample space is: $\texttt{HH}$, $\texttt{HT}$, $\texttt{TH}$, $\texttt{TT}$, each with a probability $0.25$.
- The <span style="color: purple;">joint distribution</span> of this process is the following:

|     $X/Y$     |   $\texttt{H}$   |   $\texttt{T}$    |
|:----------:|:--------:|:-------:|
|     $\texttt{H}$    |   0.25  |  0.25  |
|     $\texttt{T}$    |   0.25  |  0.25  |

![](images/two_coins.png){fig-align="center" width=10%}

### Random Variable Setup

<br>

- Let us set the following <span style="color: purple;">binary random variables</span> (since each one could only have two outcomes, $\texttt{H}$ or $\texttt{T}$):

\begin{gather*}
X = \text{First coin's outcome.} \\
Y = \text{Second coin's outcome.}
\end{gather*}

### Computing Probabilities

<br>

- Each cell of the previous joint distribution is computed as:

\begin{align*}
P(X = \texttt{H} \cap Y = \texttt{H}) &= P(X = \texttt{H}) \cdot P(Y = \texttt{H}) \qquad \text{independence} \\
&= 0.5 \cdot 0.5  \qquad \text{fair coins} \\
&= 0.25.
\end{align*}

![](images/two_coins.png){fig-align="center" width=30%}

### Can we have an univariate setup?

- <span style="color: purple;">Alternatively</span>, we can define the following random variable:

$$Z = \text{Outcomes obtained when tossing two independent coins.}$$

| Outcome | Probability |
|:------:|:------:|
| $\texttt{HH}$ | 0.25 |
| $\texttt{HT}$ | 0.25 |
| $\texttt{TH}$ | 0.25 |
| $\texttt{TT}$ | 0.25 |


### 1.1. Example: Length of Stay Versus Gang Demand

::: incremental
- We will work with the following joint distribution of <span style="color: purple;">length of stay</span> ($\text{LOS}$) of a ship and its <span style="color: purple;">gang demand</span> ($\text{Gangs}$).
- Consider an example that a Vancouver port faces with gang demand. 
- When a ship arrives, they request a certain number of gangs to unload the ship.
:::

![](images/ship.png){fig-align="center" width=30%}


#### Probability Mass Function (PMF) for Gangs

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 7

library(tidyverse)

gang <- 1:4
p <- c(0.2, 0.4, 0.3, 0.1)
tibble(
  gangs = gang,
  p = p
) |>
  ggplot(aes(gangs, p)) +
  geom_col(fill = "palegreen3") +
  labs(
    x = "Number of Gangs",
    y = "Probability"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 25, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 23),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 23, face = "bold")) 
```

#### PMF for Length of Stay

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 7

library(kableExtra)

LOS <- tribble(
  ~ ndays, ~ p,
  1, 0.25,
  2, 0.35,
  3, 0.2,
  4, 0.1,
  5, 0.1
)
LOS_PMF <- kable(LOS,
  col.names = c("LOS", "Probability"),
  align = "cc") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 40) 
LOS_PMF
```

![](images/ship.png){fig-align="center" width=15%}

#### Now, we might wonder...

<br>

> What is the probability that a ship requires 4 gangs **AND** will stay in port for 5 days?

::: incremental
- The information provided by both separate PMFs ($\text{Gangs}$ and $\text{LOS}$) is not sufficient to answer this question. 
- We would need to use a <span style="color: purple;">joint distribution</span> between $\text{LOS}$ and $\text{Gangs}$.
:::

#### Before, let us define the following:

- <span style="color: purple;">In a random system/process with more than one random variable</span>, the distribution of a standalone variable is called a <span style="color: purple;">marginal distribution</span>.

![](images/panda.png){fig-align="center" width=22%}

#### Now, going back to the joint distribution...

- We need a probability for <span style="color: purple;">every possible combination</span> of the number of $\text{Gangs}$ and $\text{LOS}$. 
- In this case, $5 \times 4 = 20$ probabilities (that again add up to 1).

```{r}
#| echo: false

raw_data <- data.frame(
  LOS = c(rep(1, 4), rep(2, 4), rep(3, 4), rep(4, 4), rep(5, 4)), Gangs = rep(1:4, 5),
  Probability = c(
    0.00170, 0.04253, 0.12471, 0.08106,
    0.02664, 0.16981, 0.13598, 0.01757,
    0.05109, 0.11563, 0.03203, 0.00125,
    0.04653, 0.04744, 0.00593, 0.00010,
    0.07404, 0.02459, 0.00135, 0.00002
  )
)

joint_distribution <- raw_data |>
  mutate(
    LOS = str_c("LOS = ", LOS),
    Gangs = str_c("Gangs = ", Gangs)
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = LOS, names_from = Gangs, values_from = Probability) |>
  column_to_rownames("LOS") |>
  as.matrix()
```

```{r}
kable(joint_distribution, align = "cccc") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 30) |>
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

#### Now, we might wonder...

<br>

> Could the 20 numbers in the joint distribution be absolutely **ANY** probabilities between 0 and 1?

::: incremental
- No, we have the following restrictions:

  + They are restricted by the fact that they will need to add up to 1 (recall the <span style="color: purple;">Law of Total Probability</span>!).
  + We need the joint distribution to be <span style="color: purple;">consistent</span> with those marginal distributions.
:::
  
### 1.2. Calculating Marginal Distributions from the Joint Distribution

- In the case of discrete random variables, we add up the probabilities of the corresponding <span style="color: purple;">standalone outcomes</span>.

```{r}
kable(joint_distribution, align = "cccc") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 30) |>
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

#### Let us start with the marginal distribution of $\text{LOS}$...

<br>

- We can compute $P(\text{LOS} = 1)$. 

. . .

- Thus, there are four ways this could happen:
  *  $\text{LOS} = 1$ and $\text{Gangs} = 1$.
  *  $\text{LOS} = 1$ and $\text{Gangs} = 2$.
  *  $\text{LOS} = 1$ and $\text{Gangs} = 3$.
  *  $\text{LOS} = 1$ and $\text{Gangs} = 4$.
  
#### So, to find the marginal probability $P(\text{LOS} = 1)$...

<br>

\begin{align*}
P(\text{LOS} = 1) &= P(\text{LOS} = 1 \cap \text{Gangs} = 1) + \\
& \quad \quad P(\text{LOS} = 1 \cap \text{Gangs} = 2) +  \\
& \quad \quad \quad P(\text{LOS} = 1 \cap \text{Gangs} = 3) + \\
& \quad \quad \quad \quad P(\text{LOS} = 1 \cap \text{Gangs} = 4) \\
&= 0.00170 + 0.04253 + 0.12471 + 0.08106 \\
&= 0.25.
\end{align*}

#### We have $P(\text{LOS} = 1)$...

- But we would also need $P(\text{LOS} = 2)$, $P(\text{LOS} = 3)$, etc.
- Thus, we add up each row from our joint distribution.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R` Code**

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "1"
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
rowSums(joint_distribution) |>
  kable(col.names = "Probability", align = "c") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 30) |>
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```


## **Output**

```{r}

#| echo: false
rowSums(joint_distribution) |>
  kable(col.names = "Probability", align = "c") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 30) |>
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

:::

####  Now for $\text{Gangs}$!

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R` Code**

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "1"
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
colSums(joint_distribution) |>
  kable(col.names = "Probability", align = "c") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 30) |>
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```


## **Output**

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
colSums(joint_distribution) |>
  kable(col.names = "Probability", align = "c") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 30) |>
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

:::

<br>

- Note both marginals computed from the joint are <span style="color: purple;">consistent</span> with our initial marginals.

## 2. Independence and Dependence Concepts

- A big part of Data Science is about <span style="color: purple;">harvesting the relationship between the variables</span> in our datasets.

![](images/cloud.jpg){fig-align="center" width=30%}

<br>

### 2.1. Independence

<br>

- Let $X$ and $Y$ be two random variables.
- $X$ and $Y$ are <span style="color: purple;">independent</span> if knowing something about one of them tells us nothing about the other:
$$P(X = x \cap Y = y) = P(X = x) \cdot P(Y = y).$$
-  We would only need the marginals to obtain their joint distribution.

#### Going back to the two coins!

- Recall we had this joint distribution:

\begin{gather*}
X = \text{First coin's outcome.} \\
Y = \text{Second coin's outcome.}
\end{gather*}

|     $X/Y$    |   $\texttt{H}$   |   $\texttt{T}$    |
|:----------:|:--------:|:-------:|
|     $\texttt{H}$    |   0.25  |  0.25  |
|     $\texttt{T}$    |   0.25  |  0.25  |

![](images/two_coins.png){fig-align="center" width=18%}

#### Obtaining the Marginals from the Joint

We can see that the two coin flips are independent:

\begin{align*}
P(X = \texttt{H}) &= P(X = \texttt{H} \cap Y = \texttt{H}) + P(X = \texttt{H} \cap Y = \texttt{T}) \\
&= 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5 \\
P(X = \texttt{T}) &= P(X = \texttt{T} \cap Y = \texttt{H}) + P(X = \texttt{T} \cap Y = \texttt{T}) \\
&= 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5 \\
P(Y = \texttt{H}) &= P(X = \texttt{H} \cap Y = \texttt{H}) + P(X = \texttt{T} \cap Y = \texttt{H}) \\
&= 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5 \\
P(Y = \texttt{T}) &= P(X = \texttt{H} \cap Y = \texttt{T}) + P(X = \texttt{T} \cap Y = \texttt{T}) \\
&= 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5.
\end{align*}

#### Applying the Independence Property via the Marginals

<br>

\begin{align*}
P(X = \texttt{H} \cap Y = \texttt{H}) &= P(X = \texttt{H}) \cdot P(Y = \texttt{H}) \\ 
&= 0.5 \cdot 0.5 = 0.25 \\
P(X = \texttt{H} \cap Y = \texttt{T}) &= P(X = \texttt{H}) \cdot P(Y = \texttt{T}) \\ 
&= 0.5 \cdot 0.5 = 0.25 \\
P(X = \texttt{T} \cap Y = \texttt{H}) &= P(X = \texttt{T}) \cdot P(Y = \texttt{H}) \\ 
&= 0.5 \cdot 0.5 = 0.25 \\
P(X = \texttt{T} \cap Y = \texttt{T}) &= P(X = \texttt{T}) \cdot P(Y = \texttt{T}) \\ 
&= 0.5 \cdot 0.5 = 0.25. 
\end{align*}

#### Let us check another two-coin case...

\begin{gather*}
X = \text{First coin's outcome} \\
Y = \text{Second coin's outcome.}
\end{gather*}

|     $X/Y$    |   $\texttt{H}$   |   $\texttt{T}$    |
|:----------:|:--------:|:-------:|
|     $\texttt{H}$    |   0.2  |  0.6  |
|     $\texttt{T}$    |   0.05  |  0.15  |

<br>

![](images/two_coins.png){fig-align="center" width=2%}

#### Computing the Marginals

<br>

\begin{align*}
P(X = \texttt{H}) &= P(X = \texttt{H} \cap Y = \texttt{H}) + P(X = \texttt{H} \cap Y = \texttt{T}) \\
&= 0.2 + 0.6 \\
&= 0.8.
\end{align*}

. . .

- By the <span style="color: purple;">Law of Total Probability</span>, we can obtain:
\begin{align*}
P(X = \texttt{T}) &= 1 - P(X = \texttt{H})\\
&= 1 - 0.8 \\
&= 0.2.
\end{align*}

#### And likewise for the second coin...

<br>

\begin{align*}
P(Y = \texttt{H}) &= P(X = \texttt{H} \cap Y = \texttt{H}) + P(X = \texttt{T} \cap Y = \texttt{H}) \\
&= 0.2 + 0.05 \\
&= 0.25.
\end{align*}

. . .

- By the <span style="color: purple;">Law of Total Probability</span>, we can obtain:
\begin{align*}
P(Y = \texttt{T}) &= 1 - P(Y = \texttt{H})\\
&= 1 - 0.25 \\
&= 0.75.
\end{align*}

#### Applying the Independence Property via the Marginals

- These two coins are also <span style="color: purple;">independent</span>!

\begin{align*}
P(X = \texttt{H} \cap Y = \texttt{H}) &= P(X = \texttt{H}) \cdot P(Y = \texttt{H}) \\ 
&= 0.8 \cdot 0.25 = 0.2 \\
P(X = \texttt{H} \cap Y = \texttt{T}) &= P(X = \texttt{H}) \cdot P(Y = \texttt{T}) \\ 
&= 0.8 \cdot 0.75 = 0.6 \\
P(X = \texttt{T} \cap Y = \texttt{H}) &= P(X = \texttt{T}) \cdot P(Y = \texttt{H}) \\ 
&= 0.2 \cdot 0.25 = 0.05 \\
P(X = \texttt{T} \cap Y = \texttt{T}) &= P(X = \texttt{T}) \cdot P(Y = \texttt{T}) \\ 
&= 0.2 \cdot 0.75 = 0.15.
\end{align*}

#### But there is no independence in this other two-coin case!

\begin{gather*}
X = \text{First coin's outcome} \\
Y = \text{Second coin's outcome.}
\end{gather*}

|     $X/Y$    |   $\texttt{H}$   |   $\texttt{T}$    |
|:----------:|:--------:|:-------:|
|     $\texttt{H}$    |   0.5  |  0  |
|     $\texttt{T}$    |   0  |  0.5  |

<br>

![](images/two_coins.png){fig-align="center" width=25%}

### 2.2. Measures of Dependence

- Let us ask ourselves the following: 

> What if two random variables <span style="color: purple;">are not</span> independent?

![](images/panda.png){fig-align="center" width=18%}

> Is there some <span style="color: purple;">measure of dependence</span>?

#### 2.2.1. Covariance and Pearson's Correlation

<br>

- <span style="color: purple;">Covariance</span> is one common way of measuring dependence between two <span style="color: purple;">numeric</span> random variables. 
- It measures the <span style="color: purple;">amount of dependence</span> and <span style="color: purple;">direction</span>:

\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) &= \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)] \\
&= \mathbb{E}(XY) - \mathbb{E}(X)\mathbb{E}(Y).
\end{align*}

#### Going back to our cargo ship example!

::: {.panel-tabset}

. . .

<br>

Thus:

$$\mathbb{E}(\text{LOS} \cdot \text{Gangs}) = 4.89956.$$

#### Computing the Covariance

<br>

\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Cov}(\text{LOS}, \text{Gangs}) &= \mathbb{E}(\text{LOS} \cdot \text{Gangs}) - \mathbb{E}(\text{LOS})\mathbb{E}(\text{Gangs}) \\
&= 4.89956 - \left[ (2.45)(2.3) \right] \\
&= -0.73544.
\end{align*}

. . .

- Indeed, we can see that the covariance between $\text{LOS}$ and $\text{Gangs}$ is <span style="color: purple;">negative</span>.
- A negative sign indicates that <span style="color: purple;">an increase in $\text{LOS}$ is associated with a decrease in $\text{Gangs}$</span>.

#### Covariance Drawback

::: incremental
- This measure depends on the <span style="color: purple;">spread</span> of the random variables $X$ and $Y$.
- For instance, if we multiply $X$ by 10, then the covariance of $X$ and $Y$ increases by a factor of 10 as well: 
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Cov}(10X,Y) &= \mathbb{E}(10XY) - \mathbb{E}(10X) \mathbb{E}(Y) \\
&= 10\mathbb{E}(XY) - 10\mathbb{E}(X)\mathbb{E}(Y) \\
&= 10[\mathbb{E}(XY) - \mathbb{E}(X) \mathbb{E}(Y)] \\
&= 10\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y).
\end{align*}
:::

#### Pearson's Correlation

::: incremental
- Pearson's correlation <span style="color: purple;">standardizes</span> the distances according to the standard deviations $\sigma_X$ and $\sigma_Y$ of $X$ and $Y$, respectively. 
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Corr}(X, Y) &= \mathbb{E} \left[ 
   \left(\frac{X-\mu_X}{\sigma_X}\right) 
   \left(\frac{Y-\mu_Y}{\sigma_Y}\right)
 \right] \\
 &= \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}.
\end{align*}
- It turns out that $-1 \leq \text{Corr}(X, Y) \leq 1$.
:::

#### Pearson's Correlation Scale

<br>

::: incremental
- $-1$ means a perfect negative linear relationship between $X$ and $Y$.
- $0$ means no linear relationship (<span style="color: purple;">however, this does not mean independence!</span>).
- $1$ means a perfect positive linear relationship.
:::

![](images/plot.png){fig-align="center" width=20%}

#### iClicker Question

<br>

Answer **TRUE** or **FALSE**:

<br>

Covariance can be negative, but not the variance.

**A.** TRUE

**B.** FALSE

![](images/panda.png){fig-align="center" width=18%}

#### iClicker Question

Answer **TRUE** or **FALSE**:

Without any further assumptions between random variables $X$ and $Y$, covariance is calculated as 

$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}(XY) - \left[ \mathbb{E}(X) \mathbb{E}(Y) \right].$$ 

Computing $\mathbb{E}(XY)$ requires the joint distribution, but computing $\mathbb{E}(X) \mathbb{E}(Y)$ only requires the marginals.

<br>

**A.** TRUE

**B.** FALSE

#### 2.2.2. Kendall's $\tau_K$

<br>

- Pearson's correlation measures <span style="color: purple;">linear dependence</span>.
- This might be a big downfall, since many relationships between real-world variables <span style="color: purple;">are not linear</span>.
- Hence, there is an alternative measure called Kendall's $\tau_K$.

![](images/plot.png){fig-align="center" width=20%}

#### Characteristics of Kendall's $\tau_K$

::: incremental
- Kendall's $\tau_K$ can measure non-linear dependence.
- It measures concordance between <span style="color: purple;">each pair</span> of observations $(x_i, y_i)$ and $(x_j, y_j)$ with $i \neq j$:
:::

. . .

<center>
**Concordant** means 
\begin{gather*}
x_i < x_j \quad \text{and} \quad y_i < y_j, \\
\text{or} \\
x_i > x_j \quad \text{and} \quad y_i > y_j;
\end{gather*}
which gets a positive sign.
</center>

#### Characteristics of Kendall's $\tau_K$

<br>

<center>
**Discordant** means 
\begin{gather*}
x_i < x_j \quad \text{and} \quad y_i > y_j, \\
\text{or} \\
x_i > x_j \quad \text{and} \quad y_i < y_j;
\end{gather*}
which gets a negative sign.
</center>

#### Formal Definition

- Kendall's $\tau_K$ <span style="color: purple;">averages the amount of concordance and discordance</span> by taking the difference between the number of concordant and number of discordant pairs. 
- The formal definition with $n$ data pairs is

$$\tau_K = \frac{\text{Number of concordant pairs} - \text{Number of discordant pairs}}{{n \choose 2}}.$$

. . .

- Kendall's $\tau_K$ is between -1 and 1, and measures dependence's strength (and direction).

#### First Example

<br>

::: incremental
- Consider the two correlation measures: Pearson and Kendall's $\tau_K$.
- We will hypothetical dataset called `non_linear_function` with $n = 21$ where:
$$y = x^{1/3}.$$
:::

#### Coding Up `non_linear_function`

<br>

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R` Code**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
non_linear_pairs <- tibble(
  x = seq(from = 0, to = 100, by = 5),
  y = x^(1 / 3)
)
non_linear_pairs
```

## **Output**

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
non_linear_pairs <- tibble(
  x = seq(from = 0, to = 100, by = 5),
  y = x^(1 / 3)
)
non_linear_pairs
```

:::

#### Plotting `non_linear_function`

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 7

ggplot(non_linear_pairs, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, colour = "dodgerblue2") +
  geom_line(colour = "dodgerblue2") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 25),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 23),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 23, face = "bold")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(from = 0, to = 100, by = 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:10) +
  ggtitle(expression(paste("Function ", 'y = ', x^{1/3})))
```

#### Computing Correlation Metrics

<br>

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R` Code**

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "3,4"
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
tribble(
  ~Pearson, ~Kendall,
  round(cor(non_linear_pairs, method = "pearson")[1, 2], 4),
  round(cor(non_linear_pairs, method = "kendall")[1, 2], 4)
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "cc")
```

## **Output**

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
tribble(
  ~Pearson, ~Kendall,
  round(cor(non_linear_pairs, method = "pearson")[1, 2], 4),
  round(cor(non_linear_pairs, method = "kendall")[1, 2], 4)
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "cc")
```

:::

#### Second Example

<br>

::: incremental
- Consider the two correlation measures: Pearson and Kendall's $\tau_K$.
- We will hypothetical dataset called `parabola_pairs` with $n = 21$ where:
$$y = x^2.$$
:::

#### Coding Up `parabola_pairs`

<br>

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R` Code**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
parabola_pairs <- tibble(
  x = seq(from = -50, to = 50, by = 5),
  y = x^2
)
parabola_pairs
```

## **Output**

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
parabola_pairs <- tibble(
  x = seq(from = -50, to = 50, by = 5),
  y = x^2
)
parabola_pairs
```

:::

#### Plotting `parabola_pairs`

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 7

ggplot(parabola_pairs, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, colour = "orangered3") +
  geom_line(colour = "orangered3") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 25),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 23),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 23, face = "bold")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(from = -50, to = 50, by = 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(from = 0, to = 2500, by = 500)) +
  ggtitle(expression(paste("Function ", 'y = ', x^2)))
```

#### Computing Correlation Metrics

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R` Code**

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "3,4"
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
tribble(
  ~Pearson, ~Kendall,
  round(cor(parabola_pairs, method = "pearson")[1, 2], 4),
  round(cor(parabola_pairs, method = "kendall")[1, 2], 4)
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "cc")
```

## **Output**

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
tribble(
  ~Pearson, ~Kendall,
  round(cor(parabola_pairs, method = "pearson")[1, 2], 4),
  round(cor(parabola_pairs, method = "kendall")[1, 2], 4)
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "cc")
```

:::

<br>

. . .

- Patterns like a parabola are not monotonically increasing or decreasing.
- Thus, neither Pearson nor Kendall's $\tau_K$ will capture the parabola pattern.

### 2.3. Variance of a Sum Involving Two Non-Independent Random Variables

<br>

- Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are <span style="color: purple;">not independent</span> random variables. 
- Therefore:
$$\operatorname{Var}(X + Y) = \operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(Y) + 2\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y).$$

#### If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then...

$$\mathbb{E}(XY) = \mathbb{E}(X) \mathbb{E}(Y).$$

. . .

- Finally: 

\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Var}(X + Y) &= \operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(Y) + 2\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) \\
&= \operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(Y) + 2 \left\{ \mathbb{E}(XY) - \left[ \mathbb{E}(X)\mathbb{E}(Y) \right] \right\} \\
&= \operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(Y) + 2 \underbrace{\left\{ \left[ \mathbb{E}(X) \mathbb{E}(Y) \right] - \left[ \mathbb{E}(X)\mathbb{E}(Y) \right] \right\}}_{0} \\
&= \operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(Y).
\end{align*}
